name: Post-Plague Economic Transformation
summary: The Black Death's destruction of one-third of Europe's labor force transforms the medieval economy. Real wages for agricultural workers roughly double in the generation after 1348; lords cannot prevent peasant migration to better-paying work; serfdom collapses in western Europe as lords cannot enforce villein obligations on mobile workers. English landlords shift from labor-intensive grain farming to sheep grazing (less labor), expanding wool exports that fund the Hundred Years' War.

_quarry.structural_significance: The plague-induced economic transformation is as important as the demographic one; the rise of real wages for common people, the weakening of servile obligations, and the shift to pastoral farming reshape the English and continental economies; the paradox of demographic catastrophe producing prosperity for survivors creates the conditions for late medieval consumer culture and the increasing domestic demand that drives craft specialization
